text.p: These are significant stories in the Nigerian press on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Nigeria pleads not guilty in Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi's alleged violation of United Nations embargo on flights from his country when he flew to Niger and Nigeria recently. Nigeria tells U.N. security council in New York that Gaddafi had been expected to travel to Nigeria by road.
- The national electricity power authority seeks an upward review of tariffs to be able meet costs of providing power.
- The number of candidates looking for admission into Nigerian universities has fallen to 360,000 in 1997 from 415,000 last year.

- Negotiations have begun in London between Nigeria and Britain to try to lift a ban each side has imposed on aircraft of the other from landing on their territory, aviation sources said. Meanwhile, other European airlines are reaping from passengers flocking to them as the ban has stopped British Airway's daily flights to Nigeria.
- Pro-democracy groups form a new coalition to scuttle an alleged plan by military ruler General Sani Abacha to transform himself into an elected president next year.
- Four indigenous companies have joined the scramble for oil exploration licences.
- The Chartered Institute of Insurance of Nigeria tells insurance firms that can not meet a new minimum capital base of 90 million naira set by the authorities to merge.
- Nigerian government is set to enter into joint ventures with local and foreign firms to exploit deposits of 450 solid mineral identified in the country.
